title: Ordinal logistic regression
biology: Coral bleaching severity along a temperature gradient
design: Independent coral fragments are assigned a four-level ordered bleaching score.
data_characteristics: Ordered categories: none, mild, moderate, severe
Distances between score levels are not assumed equal
question: Does temperature shift bleaching severity toward higher ordered categories?
null: The common temperature coefficient is zero; the modeled severity distribution does not change with temperature.
options: Mark the response as ordered in the correct direction.
exp(coefficient) compares odds of higher versus lower severity.
assumptions: A common temperature effect across cumulative thresholds is plausible.
The predictor relationship on the logit scale is appropriate.
parametric: Use partial proportional-odds or multinomial models if the common effect fails.
Use an ordinal mixed model for clustered fragments.
nonparametric: Spearman association can address monotonic ordering with a different null.
A design-based permutation test must preserve the treatment structure.

plot_args.note: Show probabilities across the temperature gradient.
Keep probabilities on their natural scale.

code_simulate:
set.seed(3115)
d <- data.frame(fragment = 1:180, temperature = runif(180, 26, 32))
latent <- .8 * (d$temperature - 28) + rlogis(180)
d$severity <- cut(latent, c(-Inf, -1, .7, 2.2, Inf),
                  labels = c("None", "Mild", "Moderate", "Severe"))
write.csv(d, file.path(out_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(plot_data, ggplot2::aes(temperature, probability,
                                            color = severity)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(values = c(None = "#6b8581", Mild = "#126887",
                                        Moderate = "#b96735", Severe = "#682b35")) +
  ggplot2::ylim(0, 1) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Predicted category probability",
                color = "Bleaching severity") +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 17) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top")
print(p)
code_analysis:
d$severity <- ordered(d$severity, levels = c("None", "Mild", "Moderate", "Severe"))
fit <- ordinal::clm(severity ~ temperature, data = d, link = "logit")
fit0 <- ordinal::clm(severity ~ 1, data = d, link = "logit")
LR <- 2 * as.numeric(logLik(fit) - logLik(fit0))
p_value <- pchisq(LR, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
b <- fit$beta["temperature"]
se <- sqrt(vcov(fit)["temperature", "temperature"])
odds_ratio <- exp(b)
ci <- exp(b + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se)
practice: Why would treating none/mild/moderate/severe as equally spaced numbers add an assumption?
generating_model: Generate 180 independent fragments with temperature Uniform(26,32) °C. Latent severity is 0.8 × (temperature - 28) plus a standard logistic error. Cut at -1, 0.7, and 2.2 to obtain None, Mild, Moderate, Severe. Do not treat category spacing as numeric distance.
generating_truth: The common temperature coefficient is 0.8, so each °C multiplies odds of higher versus lower severity by exp(0.8) ≈ 2.226 at every cumulative threshold. The zero-effect null is false and proportional odds holds by construction.

columns.name: severity
columns.meaning: Ordered bleaching level: None < Mild < Moderate < Severe

teaching_point: Ordering carries information without assuming equal distances; the common effect across thresholds is the key model assumption.
